# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been uncomfortable, but climate change has transformed it from a seasonal nuisance into a genuine public health crisis. Heat waves now kill more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and cities bear the brunt of the danger. Urban areas run several degrees hotter than their surrounding countryside—a phenomenon called the urban heat island effect—because asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb sunlight and re-radiate it long after sunset. The good news is that cities are not condemned to this fate. Through deliberate choices about trees, street design, housing, and transit, urban leaders can dramatically reduce the dangers of summer heat. The catch is that every intervention carries costs and tradeoffs, and the burden of those tradeoffs has historically fallen on the residents least equipped to bear them.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

The single most effective tool against urban heat is also the most ancient: shade. A mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath its canopy by as much as 15 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit on a scorching afternoon, not only by blocking the sun but by releasing moisture through its leaves, a process called evapotranspiration.
